newsitem.title: USA: Robust data may dim hopes for IPO market.
newsitem.headline: Robust data may dim hopes for IPO market.

text.p: Hopes for a strong September market for initial public offerings could be muted if U.S. economic growth continues to outpace estimates and inflows into equity funds remain low.

"It's going to be a lot slower than people had hoped between now and the end of the year. There's still going to be a lot of activity, but not as much as people hoped," said Michael Essex, syndicate manager at McDonald Securities.

Many firms, including TwinLab Corp., Voxware Inc., Film Roman and more, delayed planned summer IPOS until after Labour Day, betting demand would come roaring back as investors returned from vacation and the broader market picked up.
"We have about 381 deals in the pipeline (including secondary offerings) and it's on the rise," said David Menlow, president of IPO Financial Network, based in Springfield, N.J.
But the market may not be able to swallow the jump in IPOs scheduled. Robust data on the economy triggered fears of an interest rate hike and sent the market tumbling last week.
"There's a tremendous backlog ... for September. Will they all get done? I think we know the answer -- No," said Essex.
"It really depends on the economic numbers. That's what could forestall the IPO market," said Linda Intini, vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management.

"Strong numbers are a negative. If we see economic strength like the first half of the year, a lot of deals will not be priced. If we see a slowdown, the IPO market will be strong until the end of the year," she said.

"September may be critical" in terms of the supply and demand balance for equities, Gail Dudack, market strategist at UBS Securities, said in a research note. She added that inflows into domestic equity mutual funds, which can fuel demand for IPOS, have stabilised, but a much lower rate.

"It will be a buyer's market," said Essex. "Good companies with good numbers will have opportunity, but those without a good history and with capital needs are going to be at the mercy of the buyers."
Another concern for new equity deals could be third quarter "preannouncements" -- announcements by companies facing weak earnings who release the bad news early.

"Our next big number is unemployment due next week. If the interest rate environment becomes shaky and the earnings announcements are bad, that could be a thorn in the side of the IPO market," Menlow said.
"But IPOs are not going to go away. It's just going to be a selective process," he said. "There's very little going on (this) week. We'll maybe have five initial public offerings."

ML Direct Inc. is slated to go public next week. The company, which works on direct response television, including infomercials and television shopping networks, plans to offer 0.48 million shares at a maximum price of $15 each. The company has proposed to trade under the symbol "MLDR".
Also due are Rocky Mountain Internet, XOX Corp., St. Joseph Capital and Q.E.P. Co., which plans an offering of 1.2 million shares estimated to price in a range of $9.50 to $10.50 a share.
John Fitzgibbon, of the IPO Aftermarket, shrugged off concerns about interest rates, noting several possible stars in the bumper crop of deals due this month.
"Interest rate fears -- they come; they go. They're an occupational hazard," he said. "We could have as many as 100 deals in September, and some are looking interesting.

He said the Limited Inc.'s spinoff of Abercrombie & Fitch Co., sunglasses-maker Gargoyles Inc., and Infinity Financial Technology Inc. could all fetch premiums of up to two points after their market debuts.
"Sobriety came back into the marketplace and deals have lower prices. They were filed under current market conditions, with discount valuations, so we could see good performers," he said.
